title: Magnesium in Plants: What It Does and When Your Crop Needs It
metaTitle: Magnesium in Plants: Role, Signs and When It Matters
metaDescription: Magnesium in plants sits at the center of chlorophyll. See what it does, when palay, mais and fruit crops need it most, and what crowds it out.
excerpt: Magnesium in plants sits at the very center of chlorophyll, the green that turns sunlight into food, and it switches on the enzymes that move energy around the plant. A crop short of it turns yellow between the veins of its older leaves. Here is what it does, when each crop needs it most, and why too much potassium can cause its shortage.

heroImage.alt: Tomato leaf yellow between green veins: magnesium in plants running short

blocks.text:
Every molecule of chlorophyll has one atom of magnesium at its center. Without it the leaf cannot catch light, so a plant short of magnesium makes less food however much nitrogen it gets.

Magnesium also switches on the enzymes that handle ATP, the energy carrier, and it helps load sugar into the phloem so it can travel to the grain, the fruit and the roots. That is why a shortage shows late in the season as poor filling, after the crop has looked fine for weeks.
Both a building block and a helper

Magnesium works two ways. As part of chlorophyll it is a building block, held in the leaf. As the partner of ATP and many enzymes it is a helper, doing its job without being used up.

Crops take less magnesium than calcium, often 10 to 30 kilograms per hectare, but on sandy and acid soils that can be more than the soil gives.

blocks.caption: Magnesium in short
rows: The old leaves, between the veins

blocks.text:
Magnesium moves inside the plant, so the shortage starts on the older leaves. The tissue between the veins turns yellow while the veins stay green, giving a striped or marbled look, and later the yellow parts can turn reddish or die.

It is easy to confuse with potassium, which scorches the leaf edges instead, or with manganese, which starts on the young leaves. See [magnesium deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/magnesium-deficiency) to tell them apart.
When magnesium in plants is most critical

Magnesium matters most when the crop is filling: grain in palay and mais, fruit in tomato and melon, bunches in banana. Before that the leaves need it to keep making food at full speed.

DAT means days after transplanting, DAS days after sowing in the field, and DAP days after planting. The days are the usual ones for a typical variety, so a long or short variety moves them a little. Timing magnesium in plants to these windows gets more harvest from the same bags. Our guide to [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage) puts them together for a whole season.

blocks.text: What keeps magnesium from the crop

Sandy and strongly acid soils hold little magnesium and lose it in heavy rain. On other soils the trouble is competition: heavy potassium or ammonium fertilizer, or a lot of calcium from lime, crowds magnesium out at the roots.

So a field that gets plenty of muriate of potash season after season, without magnesium, can start to show the yellow stripes. Dolomite instead of plain lime fixes both the acidity and the magnesium.

Dolomite gives magnesium along with calcium and is the cheapest choice for acid soil. Magnesium sulfate, sold as Epsom salt or kieserite, dissolves quickly and works on the soil or as a leaf spray. Many complete fertilizers and foliar feeds also carry some. See [micronutrients for rice](/blog/micronutrients-for-rice) for the trace nutrients that often go with it.

items: Dolomite: magnesium and calcium, raises the pH of acid soil.
Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt, kieserite): fast magnesium with sulfur, on the soil or the leaves.
Compost and manure: small amounts released slowly.

blocks.title: Too much magnesium hurts the soil
blocks.text: Very high magnesium can make clay soil tight and slow to drain, and it crowds out potassium and calcium. Add it when a soil test or the leaves say it is short.

items.q: Is Epsom salt good for plants?
items.a: Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate, so it helps where magnesium or sulfur is short. On a soil with enough magnesium it does nothing for the crop.

items.q: What does magnesium deficiency look like?
items.a: The older leaves turn yellow between green veins, often in stripes on palay and mais. The young leaves stay green at first.

items.q: Can too much potassium cause magnesium deficiency?
items.a: Yes. Heavy potassium crowds magnesium out at the roots, most of all on sandy soil.
No. Magnesium is a secondary macronutrient, along with calcium and sulfur.
